title: Fleetwood Mac
wiki_lead:
Fleetwood Mac were a British and American  rock band formed in London in 1967. They have sold more than 120 million records worldwide, making them one of the world's best-selling musical acts. Their 1977 album, Rumours, is one of the best-selling albums of all time and won the Grammy Award for Album of the Year in 1978.  In 1979, they were honoured with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and in 1998 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and received the Brit Award for Outstanding Contribution to Music. In 2018, Fleetwood Mac received the MusiCares Person of the Year award from the Recording Academy in recognition of their artistic achievement in the music industry and dedication to philanthropy.
Primarily a British blues band in their early years, the line-up of singers/guitarists Peter Green, Jeremy Spencer and Danny Kirwan, bassist John McVie, and drummer Mick Fleetwood achieved a UK No. 1 single in 1968 with the instrumental "Albatross", and had other UK Top 10 hits with "Man of the World", "Oh Well" (both 1969), and "The Green Manalishi (With the Two Prong Crown)" (1970). Green, Spencer, and Kirwan left the band in succession during 1970–1972, with McVie's wife, singer/keyboardist Christine McVie, and American singer/guitarist Bob Welch joining during this period. 1974 saw the band's relocation to the United States and Welch's departure. Fleetwood and the McVies recruited singer/guitarist Lindsey Buckingham and singer Stevie Nicks at the end of that year, and the first album with this line-up, Fleetwood Mac (1975), topped the Billboard 200 chart in the US, followed by Rumours. 
The line-up remained stable through three more studio albums – Tusk (1979), Mirage (1982), and Tango in the Night (1987) – before Buckingham left in 1987 shortly after the latter's release, and was replaced by Billy Burnette and Rick Vito. The sole studio album from this line-up, Behind the Mask (1990), reached No. 1 in the UK, but was less successful in the US. The 1975–1987 line-up reunited for a one-off performance for the first inauguration of President Bill Clinton in 1993, before a full-scale reunion took place four years later, resulting in the band's fourth US No. 1 album, The Dance (1997), a live album marking the 20th anniversary of Rumours and the band's 30th anniversary. Christine McVie left in 1998 but rejoined in 2014. During her departure, Fleetwood, John McVie, Buckingham, and Nicks released the final Fleetwood Mac studio album, Say You Will, in 2003. In 2018, Buckingham was fired and replaced by Mike Campbell (formerly of Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers) and Neil Finn (of Split Enz and Crowded House). In 2024, two years after the death of Christine McVie, Nicks said she believed that the band would not continue.

grok_lead: Fleetwood Mac is a British-American rock band formed in London in July 1967 by guitarist Peter Green, drummer Mick Fleetwood, bassist John McVie, and guitarist Jeremy Spencer, initially rooted in the British blues tradition. The band underwent significant lineup changes, including Green's departure in 1970 due to mental health struggles and the addition of Christine McVie in 1970, Bob Welch in 1971, and later Stevie Nicks and Lindsey Buckingham in 1974, transforming it into a pop-rock ensemble known for intricate harmonies and emotional songwriting. Their 1975 self-titled album marked the start of their commercial breakthrough, but the 1977 release Rumours ârecorded amid intense personal turmoil including breakups and affairsâpropelled them to global stardom, selling over 40 million copies worldwide and topping charts for more than 30 weeks. The band's enduring success stems from a turbulent history of 19 members across six decades, with core figures like Fleetwood and the McVies providing stability amid departures driven by addiction, relationships, and creative clashes. Key albums such as Tusk (1979), an experimental double album, and Mirage (1982) followed, though internal strife led to Buckingham's exit in 1987 and Nicks' departure in 1991; reunions in the 1990s, including the live album The Dance (1997), revitalized their popularity. Fleetwood Mac has sold over 140 million records worldwide, making them one of the best-selling acts in music history, with hits like " Go Your Own Way," "Dreams," and " Landslide " defining 1970s soft rock and influencing subsequent generations. Inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1998, Fleetwood Mac's legacy reflects resilience, as they navigated Mick Fleetwood's bankruptcy in 1984, rehab stints, and further splitsâsuch as Buckingham's firing in 2018 âwhile continuing to tour until Christine McVie's death in 2022 effectively ended the classic lineup. Their music, blending blues, folk, and pop, captured the era's emotional complexity and remains culturally resonant, as evidenced by Rumours ' ongoing chart performance and billions of streams.
